messages.subject: mcmcplots
parts:
Dear Stan crew,

Congratulations on your work on Stan. We're very excited about what it means for the future of Bayesian modeling.

We see that you've been working on your own graphing code for MCMC output. We have an R package, mcmcplots, that may be relevant at this stage.

mcmcplots has some pretty useful MCMC graphing functionality, including plots of chain trace, density, autocorrelation, and caterpillar plots. It's fast, and has a host of neat features. For instance, given an object of multiple chains of multiple parameters, it can save PNG images for each parameter and collate the images into an HTML file with a table of contents. This makes for a fast visual way of sanity-checking the output of a complex run.

Attached is a screenshot of one of the mcmcplots outputs. This is a combination of trace, density, and autocorrelation into a single image. The vertical bars on the density indicate 95% CIs for each of two chains, red and blue. The plot is of a parameter delta[1], and the plot title is displayed using the greek letter delta.

The code is here: https://github.com/s-mckay-curtis/mcmcplots . You're welcome to simply use the code on open source terms, of course, but we'd also be happy to work with you to add the functionality you need to mcmcplots. Please let us know if you'd be interested in working with us so mcmcplots can grow to suit Stan.

P.S. If you'd like to kick the tires, please use the code from github. A new release including some bug fixes is imminent, but has not yet happened.

Best regards,
S. McKay Curtis and Ilya Goldin

Thanks for the note. We're about to announce
an official 1.0 release of Stan. We were just about to
release when we figured out how to improve the auto-dif
performance for densities without too much work, so we've
been pushing those changes through.

We're always happy to borrow others' code instead of
writing it ourselves.

On a practical note, Stan is BSD licensed and we're trying
to do as many calculations on the output in C++ as possible
to make it easy to port to R, Matlab and Python (and Stata).
Because R is GPL-ed, the R glue code has to be GPL.

Multi-HTML output is a great idea. I was just complaining
about how long full PDFs take to load of things like
traceplots. (They print much better due to the vector
graphics, but are a pain for simple diagnostics.)

I like your multiple-chain density plots. I have no experience
interpreting them, though -- I don't know how stable to
expect the estimated densities to be. Point estimates of
95% intervals are going to be fairly high variance with our
default option of 1000 samples/chain.

How do you set up the density estimation parameters?

What's partial autocorrelation?

Given that you have two chains, why is there only one
autocorrelation plot? We'll have four chains by default.

We're particularly concerned about calculating effective
sample size and potential scale reduction (R-hat).

I think you could get better scale on the autocorrelation
graph by removing the 0 entry (it's always 1.0).

I'd rather have titles match the names of variables in
the plot verbatim rather than try to convert to greek.

Do you handle discrete parameters? Stan doesn't do discrete
sampling (yet), but the output from R2WinBUGS (I don't know if
this is from coda) never made sense for discrete parameters.

We want to include something like a caterpillar plot for
multiple chains with 80% intervals and medians. We're fussing
with scales here -- for instance, if we have something like
the typical regression parameters case, do we put them all on
the same scale or not? We don't want to go so far as R2WinBUGS
and put everything on the same scale (as they do in their left-hand
plot).

- Bob

parts: Bob, thanks for the quick response. The replies below are all personal opinion; I do not speak for McKay, the primary creator and developer of mcmcplots (I believe he's waiting for membership approval to stan-dev).

On Saturday, June 30, 2012, Bob Carpenter wrote:
On a practical note, Stan is BSD licensed and we're trying
to do as many calculations on the output in C++ as possible
to make it easy to port to R, Matlab and Python (and Stata).
Because R is GPL-ed, the R glue code has to be GPL.
Personally, I like BSD just fine, but some mcmcplots code is derived from GPL code (e.g., the coda package), and could not be relicensed without rewriting.

Multi-HTML output is a great idea.  I was just complaining
about how long full PDFs take to load of things like
traceplots.  (They print much better due to the vector
graphics, but are a pain for simple diagnostics.)

HTML-and-PNG output is handy for diagnostics. An example is in beta-gamma-rho.zip, which I got via

mcmcplot(mymcmc, c("beta", "gamma", "rho"), random=5)

For publication, you wouldn't publish all plots of all parameters anyway, so to get vector graphics you might do

pdf("caterpillar-delta.pdf")
caterplot(mymcmc, "delta")
dev.off()

I like your multiple-chain density plots.  I have no experience
interpreting them, though -- I don't know how stable to
expect the estimated densities to be.   Point estimates of
95% intervals are going to be fairly high variance with our
default option of 1000 samples/chain.
How do you set up the density estimation parameters?

This simply uses the R density() function. It would be reasonable to parametrize mcmcplots to use any a custom density calculation.
  
What's partial autocorrelation?

McKay can give a better answer, but generally, http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_autocorrelation_function

Given that you have two chains, why is there only one
autocorrelation plot?  We'll have four chains by default.
Right now, it displays just one chain; the default is to use the first chain. I can imagine a single plot that displays all chains, differentiating by color just as the other plots do.

We're particularly concerned about calculating effective
sample size and potential scale reduction (R-hat).
If I'm not mistaken, R-hat is shown on the autocorrelation plot as the height of the dark grey rectangle (vs. the light grey background).

I think you could get better scale on the autocorrelation
graph by removing the 0 entry (it's always 1.0).
Unconventional, but interesting. I wonder what Andrew has to say.

I'd rather have titles match the names of variables in
the plot verbatim rather than try to convert to greek.
This is optional, and off by default, as in the enclosed beta-gamma-rho.zip.

Do you handle discrete parameters?  Stan doesn't do discrete
sampling (yet), but the output from R2WinBUGS (I don't know if
this is from coda) never made sense for discrete parameters.
Great question! McKay?

We want to include something like a caterpillar plot for
multiple chains with 80% intervals and medians.  We're fussing
with scales here -- for instance, if we have something like
the typical regression parameters case, do we put them all on
the same scale or not?  We don't want to go so far as R2WinBUGS
and put everything on the same scale (as they do in their left-hand
plot).

Caterpillars are already there, a sample is enclosed. See ?caterplot for more details, but in short, you can call caterplot(..., quantiles), where quantiles is a "list with two elements outer and inner. The outer element of the list should contain the quantiles of the posterior draws that will be plotted as the longer, thinner line. The inner element of the list should contain the quantiles of posterior draws that will be plotted as the shorter, thicker line. If missing, the default is to use list(outer=c(0.025,0.975),inner=c(0.16,0.84)), which corresponds to 95% and 68% credible intervals." By default, all parallel chains are collapsed into one chain before plotting.

The typical regression parameters case is misleading. You might want all intercepts on the same scale, but you probably wouldn't want all slopes on the same scale, unless you conscientiously centered and rescaled all covariates. A trick you might use here is to use different parameter names to group parameters by their scale, so all beta parameters get their own scale, all gamma parameters get their own, etc., and these would be displayed on separate plots.

Best,
Ilya


--
-- Ilya Goldin <www.pitt.edu/~goldin>

Wow, this is great.  Here are some quick thoughts:

1.  We should probably make a clear list (or maybe Bob has this list already) of the sorts of plots we want.  Roughly it goes something like this:

a.  The default (what we want as output of plot(...) of a stan object):  something that looks sort of like the right half of the current R2Winbugs plot, showing inferences for all 4 chains of all the saved quantities, using a sensible grouping so that vector and array parameters are clearly visible.

What do you think?

See you
Andrew

This is something that I've seen others talk about when monitoring MCMC convergence, so I included it in some of the plots (even though I don't find it particularly useful).  I just call the acf/pacf functions in stats to create the autocorrelation plots.  The dark grey areas on the plots are confidence intervals (as, for example, are produced in the "plot.acf" function).

The package currently doesn't handle discrete parameters, but this is another good idea to think about implementing in the future.

We want to include something like a caterpillar plot for
multiple chains with 80% intervals and medians.  We're fussing
with scales here -- for instance, if we have something like
the typical regression parameters case, do we put them all on
the same scale or not?  We don't want to go so far as R2WinBUGS
and put everything on the same scale (as they do in their left-hand
plot).

Ilya's idea of putting all parameters in a parameter "group" on the same scale might work nicely.  One of the motivations for writing the mcmcplots package was to create functions that made it easy to access different groups of parameters.  The package currently has the function "parms2plot" that tries to be smart about detecting which parameters form a group and which do not.  It could be relatively straightforward to implement a caterpillar plot that produces different scales for different parameter groups.

Ilya also noted that the caterplot function has the "quantiles" option to change the length of the intervals.  I also thought the density strips developed in Jackson (2008, "Displaying uncertainty with shading." The American Statistician, 62(4):340-347) were pretty slick, so I implemented density strips in the caterplot function with the "denstrip" option (which calls Jackson's own function and package).  The default is not to use density strips, because I don't think they are widely used (but I like them, anyway).

- Bob

(Affix project manager hat.) How are we going
to organize responsibility for RStan?

Daniel and I are in the best position to deal with
coding the mcmc::chains object (what Andrew calls
the "Stan object").

Jiqiang's leading the RStan effort and has the
infrastructure for generating the data for all the plots
we care about in place (other than perhaps smallest
posterior intervals, for which we're going to use
the R package due to the complexity of the estimator).
The complexity is mainly the integration with C++
(which is compounded by the compiled nature of Stan's models).

Ilya's proposing we treat the mcmcplots package as being
a source of MCMC graphics and that we integrate at
the level of RStan calling mcmcplots through R.
Pro: This is the cleanest break as it means we won't
be collaborating on code in the same repository. Cons: It
adds a dependency to RStan we have to keep up with.

It occurs to me that I didn't formally introduce myself other than "I tinker with mcmcplots". My apologies. I'm a postdoc at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon. This is a long and interesting list, to be clarified and prioritized in the future.

a. Similar to R2WinBUGS, something like the right half of Figure C.2 here:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/bugsR/software.pdf

(This plot is basically a vertical caterpillar with 80% CI. In figure C.2 above, the chains are collapsed, but we would make this collapsing optional so that it's possible to juxtapose the 4 chains.)

b. Diagnostic plots, for example plots of avg acceptance probability vs. log density, plots of #leapfrog steps vs log density, etc.

c. On the overview plot for each parameter, a visual display of R-hat and/or n.eff. This could use visual cues to flag parameters with problematic R-hat or n.eff values, based on some threshold.

d. The autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation plots could get omitted from the parameter overview by default.

e. The autocorrelation plot could omit lag at 0.

f. The autocorrelation plot could optionally separate chains instead of collapsing them as it does now.

g. The autocorrelation plot could automatically flag the case of chains having very different autocorrelation. Is there a test for this?

h. It would be interesting to add somewhat more intelligent default visualization behavior. For instance, if any parameters have problematic R-hat / n.eff, diagnostic plots would by default get generated for these, but not for other parameters.

i. Pluggable density function for the density plots.

j. Automatically choose decent density functions depending on the parameter type. I remember hearing that some density functions are especially appropriate for MCMC simulations.

k. Somehow handle discrete parameters, once Stan does.

--

The way mcmcplots grew up was to working from coda::mcmc.list objects.

Here's why trace plots are special and are worth hardcoding (rather than just leaving the user to draw in R):
1. If there is slow convergence, trace plots are a natural first place to look for diagnostics. (If R.hat is fine, I don't bother looking at trace plots, but when there are problems, I like to go first to the trace plots).
2. Traceplots use the parallel structure of the simulations--one color per chain. That's specific to iterative simulations. In contrast, scatterplots are simple and don't involve anything special with the chains (although I suppose we could make scatterplots showing a different color for each chain; if we wanted that, I'd support a special function such as mcmc.scatterplot to do this).
